column1: A SQL Server table can have at most {{c1::one}} PRIMARY KEY constraint.
column2:
That one key can contain several columns.
Review source

column1: Every column in a PRIMARY KEY must be {{c1::NOT NULL}}.
column2:
No component of a composite primary key can contain SQL NULL.
Review source

column1: On a disk-based rowstore table, PRIMARY KEY {{c1::NONCLUSTERED}} creates a nonclustered supporting index.
column2:
The primary key and the clustered index do not have to use the same columns.
Review source

column1: Define a parent reference with FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) {{c1::REFERENCES}} dbo.Customer(CustomerID).
column2:
The referenced columns must provide a qualifying unique key.
Review source

column1: If no referential action is specified for a SQL Server foreign key, the default is {{c1::NO ACTION}}.
column2:
A parent change that would break existing references is rejected.
Review source

column1: ON DELETE {{c1::SET DEFAULT}} assigns default values to the affected child foreign key columns.
column2:
The resulting values must still satisfy the foreign key and column nullability rules.
Review source

column1: A nullable column with a single-column UNIQUE constraint permits at most {{c1::one}} NULL value in SQL Server.
column2:
A second NULL violates the single-column uniqueness rule.
Review source

column1: A CHECK constraint rejects a candidate row when its predicate evaluates to {{c1::FALSE}}.
column2:
TRUE and UNKNOWN do not violate the CHECK predicate.
Review source

column1: The column property that rejects SQL NULL values is {{c1::NOT NULL}}.
column2:
This rule does not mean that an empty string is rejected.
Review source

column1: For a nullable numeric Salary column, {{c1::CHECK (Salary >= 20000)}} rejects non-NULL salaries below 20000.
column2:
Use a separate NOT NULL declaration if NULL must also be rejected.
Review source

column1: Use the {{c1::DEFAULT}} keyword in VALUES to explicitly request a column's configured default value.
column2:
An ordinary INSERT can also use the default by omitting the column.
Review source

column1: Name a default in a column definition with IsActive BIT {{c1::CONSTRAINT}} DF_Activity_IsActive DEFAULT(1).
column2:
The explicit name avoids different system-generated names across environments.
Review source

column1: For SQL Server BULK INSERT, specify {{c1::CHECK_CONSTRAINTS}} to validate CHECK and FOREIGN KEY constraints during the import.
column2:
Without this option, these constraint types are skipped and become untrusted.
Review source

column1: Create a standalone number generator with {{c1::CREATE SEQUENCE}} dbo.OrderNumbers START WITH 1000 INCREMENT BY 1;
column2:
The object generates numbers independently of a specific table.
Review source

column1: Set a sequence's initial returned value with {{c1::START WITH}} 1000.
column2:
The initial value must fall within the sequence's configured bounds.
Review source

column1: Set a sequence's step size with {{c1::INCREMENT BY}} 5.
column2:
A negative step produces a descending sequence, and the step cannot be zero.
Review source

column1: Define a sequence's lower bound with {{c1::MINVALUE}} 1000.
column2:
The lower bound also becomes the restart point when an ascending sequence cycles.
Review source

column1: Define a sequence's upper bound with {{c1::MAXVALUE}} 999999.
column2:
The upper bound limits the values that the sequence can issue.
Review source

column1: Enable automatic sequence wraparound with the {{c1::CYCLE}} option.
column2:
An ascending sequence wraps to its minimum, while a descending sequence wraps to its maximum.
Review source

column1: New SQL Server sequences default to {{c1::NO CYCLE}} when no cycling option is specified.
column2:
Reaching the configured boundary does not cause automatic wraparound.
Review source

column1: To use dbo.OrderNumbers as a column default, write OrderNumber BIGINT DEFAULT ({{c1::NEXT VALUE FOR}} dbo.OrderNumbers).
column2:
The sequence must exist in the same database as the table.
Review source

column1: Set a sequence's next returned value to 1000 with ALTER SEQUENCE dbo.OrderNumbers {{c1::RESTART WITH}} 1000;
column2:
Restarting can reissue values that already exist in stored rows.
Review source

column1: Change an existing sequence's step to 5 with {{c1::ALTER SEQUENCE}} dbo.OrderNumbers INCREMENT BY 5;
column2:
You do not need to recreate the sequence to change its increment.
Review source

column1: For sys.sp_sequence_get_range, declare the variable receiving @range_first_value OUTPUT as {{c1::SQL_VARIANT}}.
column2:
The output preserves the sequence's underlying numeric type inside SQL_VARIANT.
Review source

column1: If AS data_type is omitted in CREATE SEQUENCE, the sequence's data type defaults to {{c1::BIGINT}}.
column2:
Specify AS INT explicitly if an INT sequence is required.
Review source
